My point estimates across all three horizons were anchored closely to the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, reflecting a broadly neutral near-term outlook. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of roughly 90.21 was essentially a mean-reversion assumption, expecting little directional movement over such a short window and leaning on recent price stability. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the figure only marginally higher to 90.28, reflecting modest positive drift baked into the baseline trend while acknowledging that no strong directional catalyst was immediately evident. The one-month estimate of 90.75 continued that gentle upward drift, consistent with a slow-moving secular trend but without a strong conviction signal in either direction. All three estimates essentially treated the current price as the best single predictor, adjusted slightly for observed trend momentum.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spanning roughly 87.99 to 92.43 is relatively tight, capturing typical daily volatility in the underlying asset. By one week, the interval widens considerably to about 85.31 to 95.25, accounting for the accumulation of daily shocks and the increased likelihood of a meaningful directional move developing over several sessions. By one month, the interval stretches to roughly 80.52 to 100.98, nearly symmetrically around the point estimate, reflecting genuine agnosticism about whether the asset will be materially higher or lower. The widening follows a standard volatility-scaling logic, where uncertainty grows roughly with the square root of time.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic data surprises, central bank policy shifts, or geopolitical shocks that could generate outsized moves well beyond normal volatility. On the upside, a strong risk-on sentiment shift or unexpected positive fundamental news could propel the asset well above the upper bounds. On the downside, a liquidity event, a broader market selloff, or a deterioration in the fundamental backdrop could drive prices meaningfully below the lower bounds. The one-month interval in particular is wide enough to absorb moderate surprises, but a tail event — such as a financial crisis episode or an unexpected policy discontinuity — could easily breach even the 90% bounds I've stated.
